packs.title: From Rails to Lake
packs.promise: Turn Zürich’s rivers, reused buildings and lakeside gardens into discoveries of your own.

q.s: Find a conversation between two parts of a museum.
st: From a public exterior path, look at the museum’s historic building and angular modern extension. You may change viewpoints; you do not need both in one view.
Collect three pairs of visible details: an opening, a roof edge and a surface. In each pair, choose one detail from each part of the building.
Give each pair a shared job, such as bringing in light or sheltering a room. Notice how differently the two buildings do that job.
Choose the pair with the strongest contrast. Describe what you observed separately from any guess about how it was built.

q.s: Collect different uses inside a repeating frame.
st: Walk or look along a comfortable stretch of the viaduct from the public street. Choose three arches; you do not need to enter any shop.
For each arch, collect a clue to a different present-day use: a display, seating, an entrance or another visible feature. An empty or closed space is a valid observation.
Compare the repeated stone frame with what changes inside it. Choose which use seems most shaped by the arch and explain why.
Separate observed evidence from inference. A display is a clue; it does not tell you everything about the people or business inside.

q.s: Build a tiny field guide using forms rather than names.
st: Choose an open, comfortable part of the collection. Find three contrasting succulent forms: thick leaves, a rounded body, a tall stem or other shapes you can actually see.
For each, make a simple outline or written shape description. Add one visible detail that makes it different from the other two.
Read an available label or visitor explanation to learn where one plant stores water. If that information is absent, record your question rather than guessing a species or claiming a function.
Arrange your three entries from the broadest silhouette to the narrowest. Explain why the middle entry belongs there.

packs.title: Old Town Threads
packs.promise: Follow small clues through river lanes, public collections and hilltop views.

q.s: Turn three visible details into a sequence of hand actions.
st: From the public lane, look for three different made details on exteriors or public-facing displays: a joint, a curved edge, a weave, a hinge or another visible feature.
Give each detail an action verb such as join, bend, thread or turn. The verb describes your response to its form, not a claim about the actual maker or trade.
Arrange your three verbs into a short hand-action sequence. Try tiny comfortable gestures within your own space, or describe the movements in words.
Change the order once. Decide which sequence feels more like assembling something and explain what changed.

q.s: Reduce a familiar skyline to its smallest useful drawing.
st: Choose a public view of Fraumünster from Münsterhof or the nearby riverside. Find its slender spire and the larger shapes around it without entering the church.
Make a drawing using only three continuous lines, or describe three lines in words. Decide which features must survive and which can disappear.
Change your viewpoint a few comfortable steps or select a second source photograph. Make a second three-line version without adding more lines.
Compare what each version communicates. Choose the one that would help a friend recognize the outline and explain the detail you kept.

q.s: Find one word that can open two different subjects.
st: Choose an everyday word with more than one possible setting, such as light, field or home. Browse accessible public shelves or search the linked public catalogue.
Find two book titles connected with your word but belonging to different subjects. Use catalogue descriptions or subject headings to establish the difference; you do not need to read the books.
Record each title and its subject. Invent a short label for the imaginary shelf that would put them together, then explain the link in one sentence.
Finish with one question you would ask after reading both. No borrowing, registration, full-text access or paid service is required for the catalogue version.
